questions.q: Write and simplify the auxiliary equation for $2y'' + 4y' - 6y = 0$.
questions.answer: $2r^2 + 4r - 6 = 0$, which simplifies to $r^2 + 2r - 3 = 0$.

questions.q: Explain why substituting $y=e^{rx}$ into $ay''+by'+cy=0$ produces the auxiliary equation $ar^2+br+c=0$.
questions.answer: $y=e^{rx}$ gives $y'=re^{rx}$ and $y''=r^2e^{rx}$. Substituting: $ar^2e^{rx}+bre^{rx}+ce^{rx}=0$, i.e., $e^{rx}(ar^2+br+c)=0$. Since $e^{rx}\ne0$ for all $x$, this forces $ar^2+br+c=0$.
$r^2-5r+6=(r-2)(r-3)=0 \Rightarrow r = 2, 3$. General solution: $y = C_1e^{2x} + C_2e^{3x}$.
$r^2-r-6=(r-3)(r+2)=0 \Rightarrow r=3,-2$. General solution: $y=C_1e^{3x}+C_2e^{-2x}$.

questions.q: Solve $y'' - 9y = 0$ (note this factors as a difference of squares in $r$).
questions.answer: $r^2-9=(r-3)(r+3)=0 \Rightarrow r=\pm3$. General solution: $y=C_1e^{3x}+C_2e^{-3x}$.
$r^2-6r+9=(r-3)^2=0 \Rightarrow r=3$ (repeated). General solution: $y = (C_1+C_2x)e^{3x}$.

questions.q: Explain why, for a repeated root $r$, $y_2=xe^{rx}$ (not just a second copy of $e^{rx}$) is needed to build the general solution.
questions.answer: $y_1=e^{rx}$ and a constant multiple of it, $ce^{rx}$, are linearly dependent — they don't give two independent solutions needed for a second-order equation's two-dimensional solution space. Direct substitution confirms $y_2=xe^{rx}$ also solves the ODE when $r$ is a repeated root, and $y_1,y_2$ are linearly independent (their Wronskian is $e^{2rx}\ne0$), so together they span the full solution space.
$r^2+4=0 \Rightarrow r=\pm 2i$. General solution: $y = C_1\cos 2x + C_2\sin 2x$.
$r^2-2r+5=0 \Rightarrow r=\dfrac{2\pm\sqrt{4-20}}{2}=1\pm 2i$. General solution: $y = e^{x}(C_1\cos 2x + C_2\sin 2x)$.
$r^2+9=0 \Rightarrow r=\pm3i$. So $y=C_1\cos3x+C_2\sin3x$. $y(0)=C_1=2$. $y'=-3C_1\sin3x+3C_2\cos3x$; $y'(0)=3C_2=3 \Rightarrow C_2=1$. Thus $y=2\cos3x+\sin3x$.
$r^2+2r+2=0 \Rightarrow r=\dfrac{-2\pm\sqrt{4-8}}{2}=-1\pm i$. General solution: $y=e^{-x}(C_1\cos x+C_2\sin x)$.

questions.q: Without solving, state whether $y'' + 6y' + 5y = 0$ has real, repeated, or complex roots, using the discriminant $b^2-4ac$ of the auxiliary equation.
questions.answer: Discriminant $=36-20=16>0$ and a perfect square, so the roots are real and distinct ($r=-1,-5$).

questions.q: Without solving, classify the roots of $y'' + 10y' + 25y = 0$.
questions.answer: Discriminant $=100-100=0$, so the auxiliary equation has one repeated real root ($r=-5$).

questions.q: Without solving, classify the roots of $y'' + 2y' + 10y = 0$.
questions.answer: Discriminant $=4-40=-36<0$, so the roots are complex conjugates ($r=-1\pm3i$).

questions.q: A mass–spring–damper system satisfies $y'' + 4y' + 5y = 0$. Find the general solution and classify the damping (over/critically/under-damped).
questions.answer: $r^2+4r+5=0$, discriminant $=16-20=-4<0$, so $r=-2\pm i$. General solution: $y = e^{-2x}(C_1\cos x + C_2\sin x)$ — this is under-damped (complex roots with negative real part give oscillatory decay).

$r^2+6r+9=(r+3)^2=0 \Rightarrow r=-3$ (repeated) — critically damped. So $y=(C_1+C_2x)e^{-3x}$. From $y(0)=1$: $C_1=1$. $y'=C_2e^{-3x}-3(C_1+C_2x)e^{-3x}$; $y'(0)=C_2-3C_1=0 \Rightarrow C_2=3$. Thus $y=(1+3x)e^{-3x}$.

$r^2+5r+6=(r+2)(r+3)=0 \Rightarrow r=-2,-3$ (real, distinct, both negative) — over-damped. So $y=C_1e^{-2x}+C_2e^{-3x}$. $y(0)=C_1+C_2=1$. $y'=-2C_1e^{-2x}-3C_2e^{-3x}$; $y'(0)=-2C_1-3C_2=0 \Rightarrow C_1=-\frac{3}{2}C_2$. Substituting: $-\frac{3}{2}C_2+C_2=1 \Rightarrow -\frac{1}{2}C_2=1 \Rightarrow C_2=-2$, $C_1=3$. Thus $y=3e^{-2x}-2e^{-3x}$.

questions.q: For the general damped spring equation $my''+cy'+ky=0$ ($m,c,k>0$), explain in one sentence why the real part of every root of the auxiliary equation is always negative (so every solution decays).
questions.answer: By the quadratic formula the roots are $r=\dfrac{-c\pm\sqrt{c^2-4mk}}{2m}$: when the roots are real, $\sqrt{c^2-4mk} < c$ (since $mk>0$), so both roots stay negative after adding $-c$ and dividing by $2m>0$; when complex, the real part is exactly $-\dfrac{c}{2m}<0$ since $c,m>0$ — either way the exponential factor $e^{-(c/2m)x}$ (or the two negative real exponentials) forces every solution toward $0$ as $x\to\infty$.

sections.heading: Verifying general solutions and the superposition principle

questions.q: Verify by direct substitution that $y=C_1e^{2x}+C_2e^{3x}$ solves $y''-5y'+6y=0$ for any constants $C_1,C_2$.
State the superposition principle for a linear homogeneous ODE, and explain why it guarantees that $y=C_1y_1+C_2y_2$ solves $ay''+by'+cy=0$ whenever $y_1,y_2$ each do.
questions.answer: If $y_1,y_2$ both solve $ay''+by'+cy=0$, then so does any linear combination $C_1y_1+C_2y_2$, because the operator $y\mapsto ay''+by'+cy$ is linear: $a(C_1y_1+C_2y_2)''+b(\cdots)'+c(\cdots) = C_1(ay_1''+by_1'+cy_1)+C_2(ay_2''+by_2'+cy_2)=C_1(0)+C_2(0)=0$.

questions.q: Find the auxiliary equation's roots for $y''-4y=0$, then verify that both $y=e^{2x}$ and $y=e^{-2x}$ individually satisfy the ODE.

questions.answer: $r^2+1=0 \Rightarrow r=\pm i$, so $y=C_1\cos x+C_2\sin x$. $y(0)=C_1=0$. $y(\pi/2)=C_2\sin(\pi/2)=C_2=3$. Thus $y=3\sin x$.

$r^2-1=0 \Rightarrow r=\pm1$, so $y=C_1e^{x}+C_2e^{-x}$. $y(0)=C_1+C_2=1$. $y(1)=C_1e+C_2e^{-1}=e$. From the first equation, $C_2=1-C_1$; substituting: $C_1e+(1-C_1)e^{-1}=e \Rightarrow C_1(e-e^{-1})=e-e^{-1} \Rightarrow C_1=1$, so $C_2=0$. Thus $y=e^{x}$.

questions.q: Explain why the boundary value problem $y''+4y=0$, $y(0)=0$, $y(\pi)=1$ has NO solution, while $y(0)=0$, $y(\pi/4)=1$ does.
questions.answer: General solution: $y=C_1\cos2x+C_2\sin2x$. $y(0)=C_1=0$, so $y=C_2\sin2x$. At $x=\pi$: $\sin2\pi=0$, so $y(\pi)=0$ for every $C_2$ — the condition $y(\pi)=1$ can never be met. At $x=\pi/4$: $\sin(\pi/2)=1\ne0$, so $C_2=1$ solves $y(\pi/4)=1$ uniquely.
